question: Why does HeyGen say Avatar 6 is 84.4% of the way to being indistinguishable from real video?

rungs.question: Why is the number 84.4% when raters picked Avatar 6 as real only 42.2% of the time?
rungs.answer: HeyGen defines its own score: in a two-choice test, 50% is what pure guessing gives, so it doubles the share of choices that picked the avatar as real. 114 of 270 choices is 42.2%, and doubled that is 84.4%. A score of 100% would mean raters could not tell the two apart at all.

evidence.quote: Side by side with the real recording, raters pick Avatar 6 as the real one 42.2% of the time. 50% would mean they cannot tell at all, so Avatar 6 is 84.4% of the way there.
We report this as the indistinguishability rate, twice the share of choices that pick the Avatar 6

counter.text: Both sites carry HeyGen's own words (its research page and its report PDF), so the two sources share one publisher. The 270 answers also leave out the raters who said they could not tell: the report says "a further 11.2% of the 304 side-by-side answers were “can’t tell”."

rungs.question: Why were raters choosing close to chance in the side-by-side test?
rungs.answer: The test was built so only the picture differed. Each HeyGen employee's real recording was split: Avatar 6 learned from one part and generated the other, then raters saw the real and generated clip saying the same sentence over the same audio. 20 external raters judged pairs from 76 people, about four raters per pair.

counter.text: When clips were shown one at a time, raters still separated them: "Shown alone, Avatar 6 with the person’s own voice is judged real in 65.1% of answers, against 78.9% for" real recordings. The people filmed were HeyGen employees, and the report does not say how the 20 raters were recruited.

rungs.question: Why does Avatar 6 score so much higher than HeyGen's previous model, Avatar V, at 44.4%?
rungs.answer: HeyGen's reports describe Avatar 6 as building on Avatar V's approach of learning a person from a short video of them, not one photo, capturing how they speak and move as well as how they look. The reports set the two scores side by side but do not tie the gain to any one change.

measured the same way, Avatar V reaches 44.4% (22.2% picked as real) in its technical report [1].

counter.text: The two tests differ in size. Avatar V's figure came from a much smaller test: "Table 4 Avatar Turing Test results. Three annotators each evaluated 18 pairs of Avatar V outputs and ground truth", 54 judgments in all, against 270 choices from 20 raters for Avatar 6.

rungs.question: Why should the 84.4% hold outside HeyGen's own test?
rungs.answer: Nothing read answers this. Every figure for the test comes from HeyGen's own reports. OpenRouter and the csuite.so roundup list Avatar 6's release and prices but repeat none of the test, and neither describes a test run by anyone else.

counter.text: none found; scope: the five given sources plus HeyGen's Avatar V research page, which the Avatar 6 report cites. OpenRouter says "Avatar 6 was released on November 17, 2026." and csuite.so says it was "listed both on November 17, at $0.10 a second for 1080p and $0.145 for 2K, with Turbo at $0.05 and $0.0875.", with no test results.

landing.shows: The 84.4% is HeyGen's own score, made by doubling the 42.2% of side-by-side choices (114 of 270) that took Avatar 6 for the real recording. The test kept the real audio and the same sentence, used HeyGen employees' own footage and left out 11.2% of answers that said they could not tell. Shown alone, real clips were still judged real more often (78.9% against 65.1%). The jump from Avatar V's 44.4% compares a 270-choice test with a 54-judgment one, and no source read reports anyone outside HeyGen running the test.
landing.open_question: If the same side-by-side test were run by someone outside HeyGen, with strangers' footage and the "can't tell" answers counted, what share of choices would pick Avatar 6 as real?
